extracted.intended_audience: writers, playwrights, philosophers, and students of comedy/humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical analysis of what makes situations, words, and actions comic; identifies archetypal mechanisms (e.g., repetition, manipulation, escalation) and how to produce comic effects on stage or in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: We laugh every time a person gives us the impression of being a thing
rubrics_metrics.description: WE LAUGH EVERY TIME A PERSON GIVES US THE IMPRESSION OF BEING A THING.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sancho Panza tossed like a football, Baron Munchausen as a cannon-ball, circus clowns becoming rubber balls or wooden dummies. Comic effect arises when a human being is perceived as an object/thing (rigid, mechanical), often via gradual transformation or concentrated attitudes and movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual passing from the dim and vague to the clear (method of suggestion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gradual passing from the dim and vague to the clear and distinct is the method of suggestion par excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: make perceptions increasingly indefinite, then slowly solidify an image (as in hypnotic suggestion or falling-asleep images) so that the audience's imagination 'fills in' a transformed, often object-like image (e.g., doll-image from rhythmic repetition/assonance). Examples: Regnard lines and Figaro's rapid piling of epithets that suggest a doll or animal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talking about persons as one would about mere things
rubrics_metrics.description: Many amusing effects are obtained by talking about persons as one would do about mere things, or by confusing person with function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Labiche's inventory-like listing (Perrichon counting parcels then family members); confusing a prefect with the office rather than the person ('changed several times since 1847'). This partial identification (person→function/thing) suffices to produce comic suggestion without full dehumanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: illusion of life + impression of mechanical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: ANY ARRANGEMENT OF ACTS AND EVENTS IS COMIC WHICH GIVES US, IN A SINGLE COMBINATION, THE ILLUSION OF LIFE AND THE DISTINCT IMPRESSION OF A MECHANICAL ARRANGEMENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central formal definition: comedy juxtaposes apparent living continuity with detectable mechanism (strings, springs, gears). Use combinations of acts/events that simultaneously evoke life and reveal mechanical automatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Something mechanical in something living
rubrics_metrics.description: SOMETHING MECHANICAL IN SOMETHING LIVING: the comic arises from detecting rigid mechanism within the living continuity of human affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological source: this mechanicality appears as a kind of absentmindedness in life. Laughter functions as a social corrective that singles out and represses this inelasticity/automatism. Practical implication: emphasize traits or patterns that make characters seem inelastic, automatic, or puppet-like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jack-in-the-box (repetition/tempo) as a comic archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jack-in-the-box image: a bent-and-released spring; repetition producing a regular tempo and rebound (up and down) is comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage/writing application: create a recurring action or phrase with increasing emphasis/tempo so the character seems to spring up mechanically. Examples: Punch and Judy, Moliere scenes (Purgon/Argan; Sganarelle/Pancrace), where repetition marks a tempo and the 'rebound' becomes the focus of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic repetition of words: repressed feeling vs repressing idea
rubrics_metrics.description: IN A COMIC REPETITION OF WORDS WE GENERALLY FIND TWO TERMS: A REPRESSED FEELING WHICH GOES OFF LIKE A SPRING, AND AN IDEA THAT DELIGHTS IN REPRESSING THE FEELING ANEW.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret repeated phrases not as funny in themselves but as symbols of an internal mechanical conflict (e.g., Dorine/Orgon 'Et Tartuffe?', Alceste's 'I don't say that!'). Use repetition to reveal an internal duel or automated impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dancing-Jack (manipulation/personified strings) as a comic archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dancing-Jack: a character who seems to act freely but, from a viewpoint, appears as a toy whose strings are pulled by another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: present a character vacillating or controlled by external forces (other characters, fate), often by personifying opposing decisions. Examples: Scapin manipulating masters/servants; depicting choices as separate 'actors' holding the strings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personify opposing decisions to generate comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character vacillates between contrary opinions, a comic author personifies the two opposing decisions so the character appears like a marionette between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic device: externalize inner conflict as discrete, mechanical forces or figures; the audience instinctively 'takes the side' that feels more playful (e.g., Panurge asking Tom, Dick, and Harry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Snow-ball (arithmetical progression / escalation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Snow-ball: a small cause sets off a chain-reaction that grows by arithmetical progression, culminating in a large unexpected effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a minor incident that triggers successive linked consequences (toy soldiers, house of cards, a lost hat) to produce accelerating comic effect. Examples: law-suits within law-suits (Chicanneau), Labiche's straw hat that 'must' be recovered and keeps eluding capture, La Cagnotte circular returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversibility/circular return enhances comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A mechanical combination is often REVERSIBLE; circularity (return to starting-point) or the ball returning after havoc increases laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure scenes so effort or journey returns characters to where they began (ironic futility), or arrange causes/effects so they loop back, emphasizing wasted effort or fate's machinery (examples: Labiche plays where characters return to initial state).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition, Inversion, and Reciprocal Interference of Series are the fundamental comic processes
rubrics_metrics.description: From the contrasts between life and mechanism the three counterpart processes are deduced: REPETITION, INVERSION, and RECIPROCAL INTERFERENCE OF SERIES; these are the methods of light comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition is elaborated (see 'Jack-in-the-box' and 'Repetition' entries). Inversion and reciprocal interference are presented as the other two essential modes (reverse orders, series that interfere with one another) and should be used as archetypal combinatory patterns when inventing comic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition of a situation is comic when complex and naturally introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitions produced on the stage are the more laughable in proportion as the scene repeated is more complex and more naturally introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for playwrights: reconcile complexity and naturalness when repeating a scene (e.g., Ecole des femmes, George Dandin): produce iterations in distinct 'tempi' or with different groups (masters vs servants) to heighten comic symmetry without breaking plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effect can come from partial identification (function replacing person)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unnecessary to complete identification of the person with a thing; beginning to confound person with their function already produces comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metonymy or bureaucratic, inventory-like language to liken people to their roles or to impersonal objects/events (examples: Perrichon listing family/parcels; 'kings of France that have occurred' likening kings to impersonal events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic arises from 'absentmindedness' of life; laughter as a social corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigid mechanism detected in life is of peculiar interest as being a kind of ABSENTMINDEDNESS on the part of life; laughter is a social gesture that singles out and represses this absentmindedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory-to-practice: stage or write scenes that expose lapses of attention, automatism, or social inelasticity; position laughter as communal response that 'corrects' the mechanical failing by ostracizing or mocking it.
